lesson.title: The Declaration of Sentiments: Launching Organized Feminism at Seneca Falls
lesson.summary: In July 1848, a small upstate New York town hosted the first women's rights convention in American history, producing a document that reworked the Declaration of Independence to demand equality for women.
lesson.body:
By the 1840s, thousands of American women had spent a decade working in the abolitionist movement, circulating petitions, raising money, and organizing local antislavery societies. That experience taught them how to build a public campaign, but it also exposed a painful irony. In 1840, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott traveled to London for the World Anti-Slavery Convention only to be denied seats on the convention floor because they were women, forced instead to sit in a curtained gallery and watch the proceedings in silence. The insult stayed with both women for years and planted the idea that the struggle against slavery and the struggle for women's rights were connected.

That idea became action in the summer of 1848. Stanton, now living in Seneca Falls, New York, reconnected with Mott, and together with Mary Ann M'Clintock, Martha Coffin Wright, and Jane Hunt, all Quaker or Quaker connected women active in reform circles, they decided almost on impulse to call a public convention on women's rights. They placed a small unsigned notice in the Seneca County Courier and had barely a week to prepare. On July 19 and 20, 1848, roughly three hundred people, most of them women but including a substantial number of men, crowded into the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls for the first women's rights convention held anywhere in the United States.

The convention's central achievement was the Declaration of Sentiments, drafted mainly by Stanton using the Declaration of Independence as her template. Where Jefferson had written that all men are created equal, Stanton wrote that all men and women are created equal, and where the original Declaration had listed grievances against King George III, Stanton listed grievances against men in general: laws that gave husbands control over a wife's property and wages, the denial of higher education and most professions to women, and the exclusion of women from voting and from full participation in churches and public life.

Eleven resolutions followed the Declaration, and ten passed without serious debate. The eleventh, demanding the right to vote, was far more controversial, since even many reformers considered suffrage impractical or too radical to press. It passed only after Frederick Douglass, the former slave and abolitionist editor who attended the convention, spoke forcefully in its favor, arguing that the ballot was the foundation of all other rights. Sixty eight women and thirty two men ultimately signed the Declaration of Sentiments, a small number that newspapers across the country mocked mercilessly in the following weeks.

Seneca Falls did not create a mass movement overnight. Many signers, embarrassed by the ridicule, later asked to have their names withdrawn, and organized women's rights activity remained thin through the early 1850s. What the convention did accomplish was to establish a founding document and a small but committed network of leaders who would keep organizing conventions in the years that followed. Because that network grew directly out of abolitionist organizing and used its language of natural rights and moral conscience, the two reform movements would remain closely intertwined, for better and eventually for worse, as the next generation of activists would discover.
